abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable electricity generation creates opportunities for flexible demand-side energy management in Total Controlled Environment Agriculture (TCEA), where artificial lighting represents a major operational cost. However, the biological consequences of demand-responsive lighting strategies remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether photoperiods can be dynamically adjusted to minimise economic costs or maximise renewable energy utilisation while maintaining crop productivity. Using historical electricity market and wind-generation data, we evaluated three demand-flexing strategies: short-term demand-side response (DSR) events, cost-optimised photoperiods aligned with low electricity prices, and wind-optimised photoperiods aligned with periods of high renewable generation. Despite substantial variation in photoperiod length, plants maintained robust circadian rhythms under both cost- and wind-optimised regimes, demonstrating considerable resilience of the circadian system to irregular environmental timing. Commercial-scale trials involving basil, lettuce, mustard greens and rocket revealed that demand-flexed lighting regimes had minimal effects on harvested fresh or dry weight. Our findings demonstrate that TCEA can provide meaningful demand-side flexibility and support renewable energy integration without substantial reductions in crop productivity. Circadian resilience appears to buffer plants against fluctuating photoperiods, providing a biological foundation for the deployment of demand-flexible lighting strategies in future low-carbon agricultural systems.
